reading.body:
Inception's Mercury line is API only, text only, and closed weights, with the newer Mercury 2.5 both cheaper and larger in context than Mercury 2.

The family has two live versions. Mercury 2 shipped 2026-03-04 with a 128,000 token context and 50,000 token maximum output, priced at $0.25 per million input tokens and $0.75 per million output. Mercury 2.5 shipped 2026-09-08 with a 260,000 token context and 65,536 token maximum output, priced at $0.04 and $0.15. A preview build of 2.5 appeared on 2026-08-31 and is now delisted. Both live versions support reasoning.

The direction of travel within a single family is the point. In roughly six months the context window doubled, the output ceiling rose, and the price fell by more than six times on input and five times on output. For AI specifically, that combination is what makes long document work routine rather than a budget decision. A 260,000 token context at four cents per million input tokens means a reader can put a large corpus in front of the model and still afford to iterate.

What the data does not cover is anything about the compute behind these models. There are no parameter counts, no training details, no hardware, no data center or power figures, and no benchmarks. It also does not say whether Mercury 2.5 replaced Mercury 2 in capability or only in price, since no evaluation results are listed. The pricing and context numbers describe what a buyer gets at the API, not what it cost to build or where it runs.

paragraphs: Inception Mercury is a family of language models from the developer Inception. The pages describe Mercury 2 as the world's fastest reasoning language model, built to make production AI feel instant, and Mercury 2.5 as Inception's most capable production model yet, a step up in quality over Mercury 2 with the same low-latency, low-cost serving profile. Inception says Mercury 2.5 is the most capable diffusion LLM on the market and, to its knowledge, the largest diffusion language model ever trained. The family also includes Mercury Coder, which the pages call the first commercial diffusion Large Language Model (dLLM), and previews of Mercury Voice, a dLLM optimized for voice agents, and Mercury Router, which routes prompts to the best models.

Inception says the models are for latency-sensitive workloads. The pages name search agents and RAG pipelines, voice agents and interactive applications, coding subagents and assistants, agentic loops, and enterprise workflows. Mercury 2.5 is offered with 260K tokens of context, tunable reasoning, parallel tool calls, and schema-aligned JSON, at $0.20 per million input and $0.75 per million output, with a launch price of $0.04 per million input and $0.15 per million output. Mercury 2 is listed with 128K context, native tool use, and schema-aligned JSON output, at $0.25/1M input tokens and $0.75/1M output tokens. Mercury models are available through the Inception API, Baseten, and OpenRouter, and Mercury 2 is available on Azure AI Foundry in the US and Canada regions, with enterprise deployments supporting dedicated capacity, autoscaling, compliance controls, and configurable data retention.

price_limits.summary: Across the 2 versions, input prices run from $0.04 to $0.25 per million tokens and output prices from $0.15 to $0.75. Mercury 2.5 is the cheapest, at $0.04 per million input tokens and $0.15 per million output tokens. Mercury 2.5 has the largest context window, 260,000 tokens.

family_reading.text: Inception Mercury is an API only, text in and text out line with two versions, both supporting reasoning and neither publishing open weights. Context windows run from 128000 to 260000 tokens, and maximum output runs from 50000 to 65536 tokens, so long documents and long answers are both workable. The newer Mercury 2.5 is far cheaper, at $0.04 per million input and $0.15 output, against $0.25 and $0.75 for Mercury 2, and it also carries the larger context window. The facts suggest the family suits text reasoning tasks where a large context and a low price matter, such as summarising or analysing long documents. Limits are the text only input and output, the absence of open weights, and the fact that pricing and capability differ sharply between the two versions, so the older one is the costly choice.
